seo.title: Karmic tail 9 9 9 compatibility: a solitude made for two
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 9 9 compatibility: why three Hermits appear only in a couple, what the entry, middle and main task mean, and how not to hide from each other.

title: The 9-9-9 karmic tail in compatibility: three Hermits at one table
short: No single person can have three Hermits in a row: in a personal matrix The Moon always stands between two nines, because 9 + 9 = 18. The 9-9-9 tail forms only in a couple — and four times out of five in two people whose personal tails hold neither The Hermit nor The Moon. It is a tail of solitude for two: a quiet that neither partner had on their own is something they create together, and the main task is not to hide from each other inside it.

sections.h2: The riddle of the 9-9-9 tail: where did The Moon go?
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is not chosen: it is calculated from the two outer numbers. The middle N is the entry M plus the main task D. If both the entry and the task are Hermits, the middle has to be 9 + 9 = 18, which is The Moon. That is why in a single person a tail with nines at both ends looks like 9-18-9: between two Hermits there is always a fog.

A couple works by another rule. Each of its points is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22, and the middle is added up from the partners' middles, not from the ends. So in a couple the middle can stay a nine, and the 9-9-9 tail becomes possible even though no individual has it. It occurs in roughly one couple in 40 (2.489%), tenth place among the 97 couple tails.

The Moon does not vanish, though. It moves. In 92.3% of couples with this tail The Moon sits in the centre of the couple's matrix — in the atmosphere, in what happens between the partners when nobody is watching. The fog that in one person would lie in the middle of the road hangs, in a couple, in the air between two. In the remaining 7.7% the centre is The Hermit too, and then there are four nines.

There is a second clue. Lisovskaya advises adding up energies that repeat. Two Hermits make 18 — the very Moon that stands in the centre. Three Hermits make 27 → 9, The Hermit again. This tail lets no new card out of itself: the sum of its numbers comes straight back to it, like a room with no door. The couple will have to cut that door themselves.

sections.h2: A quiet made out of noise
paragraphs: The 9-9-9 tail is built from ten combinations of personal tails. The most common is 12-16-4 in one partner and 15-20-5 in the other: 54% of these couples are made this way. Another 14% are 18-6-6 and 9-3-21, and 12% are 21-4-10 and 6-5-17.

The most common combination deserves a closer look. One partner's tail holds The Hanged Man, The Tower and The Emperor; the other's holds The Devil, Judgement and The Hierophant. Six cards of drama and order: suspension, collapse, power, dependence, a loud call, law. Not a single Hermit. But add them place by place and you get 12 + 15 = 27 → 9, 16 + 20 = 36 → 9 and 4 + 5 = 9. Each number of one partner completes the other's number to a nine: the sums 27, 36 and 9 all reduce to the same card. Two noisy tails cancel each other out into quiet.

This is not an exception but the rule. Our run of every date through the site's engine shows that in 79% of couples with the 9-9-9 tail, neither partner has a 9 or an 18 anywhere in their personal tail, and in the remaining 21% both have one, and only at the personal entry. In the partners' personal middles and personal main tasks, 9 and 18 do not occur in any of the ten combinations.

Hence a conclusion worth remembering in every quarrel: the Hermit of the middle and of the main task belongs to neither of the two. It cannot be "brought into the couple" — it is born only from adding two numbers that did not contain it. The question "which of us is the closed one?" has no answer in this tail.

Wen makes a comparison that fits the most common combination surprisingly well: "Key 5: The Hierophant is about orthodox wisdom; Key 9 is the unorthodox solitary path to wisdom." The Hierophant is accepted wisdom; The Hermit is one's own untrodden way to it. In the most common combination the partners' personal main tasks are The Emperor and The Hierophant, two cards of established order. Together they give the couple's main task — The Hermit: the rules each brought from their own life add up to a path that no rulebook contains.

sections.h2: Two people at one table: Pierre and Marie Curie
paragraphs: Pierre Curie was twenty-two when he wrote in his diary: "Women, much more than men, love life for life's sake. Women of genius are rare." When, "pushed by some mystic love", a man gives all his thoughts to a work that takes him away from those around him, he wrote, "it is with women that we have to struggle, and the struggle is nearly always an unequal one. For in the name of life and of nature they seek to lead us back." He called his path "a life opposed to nature". The diary note is less about women than about a fear every Hermit knows: that closeness will pull you back into ordinary life. Pierre did not marry until he was thirty-six: he did not believe in a marriage where he would not have to choose between a person and the work.

In the spring of 1894, at the home of a Polish physicist she knew, Marie Skłodowska saw him standing in the recess of a French window. She remembered his speech, "rather slow and deliberate", his smile, "at once grave and youthful", and "the slight suggestion of detachment in his whole attitude". The conversation turned to science straight away. That summer she went home to Poland and might never have come back. Pierre wrote to her:

"We have promised each other (haven't we?) at least a great friendship. […] It would be a beautiful thing, in which I hardly dare believe, to pass through life side by side, hypnotized by our dreams: your dream for your country, our dream for humanity, our dream for science" (our translation from the French).

A year later, in July 1895, they married — with no white dress, no gold ring, no church service and no wedding breakfast. Marie asked that the dress she was given be "practical and dark, so that I can put it on afterwards to go to the laboratory". With money sent as a present by a cousin they bought two bicycles and rode off on them on a honeymoon along the roads around Paris.

They barely furnished their flat of three tiny rooms: they turned down the sofa and armchairs that Pierre's father offered, because every extra object would need dusting and there was no time for that. Their daughter Ève later described the flat: a white wooden table, Marie's chair at one end, Pierre's at the other, and between them a petroleum lamp, books on physics and a bunch of flowers. There was no third chair. The couple had agreed to do without calls and visits, and a guest who did climb the steep stairs, faced with two chairs "neither of which was for him", soon fled.

"The great thing," Marie recalled, "was that we were alone together in the little home which gave us a peace and intimacy." In eleven years together they were hardly ever apart — so rarely that almost no letters between them survive.

We have not calculated the Curies' dates, and their story here is not proof but a mirror. Still, all three nines of the tail show up in it in turn. Marie Curie's Pierre Curie (1923) and her autobiographical notes are quoted in the translation by Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg, the scenes come from Madame Curie (1937), the biography written by their younger daughter Ève, in Vincent Sheean's translation; where the English drifts from the French, the translation is ours.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: an agreement about quiet
paragraphs: The entry to the task (M) is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. On the site the same point also appears in the relationship line, under the label "Common language". Lisovskaya warns that the point lies on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. With The Hermit at the entry, a couple agrees on quiet: on a wish for depth, for a corner of their own, for the right not to explain themselves to the world.

What such a common language sounds like can be seen on one Sunday morning at the Curies'. Pierre had read a letter from technicians in Buffalo who wanted to exploit radium in America and asked how it was prepared. He calmly laid out two choices for his wife: publish everything without reserve, or patent the technique and hold the rights to radium all over the world. Marie thought for a few seconds: "It is impossible. It would be contrary to the scientific spirit." Pierre agreed, but did not want to decide lightly, and honestly named the price: their life was hard, they had a daughter, a patent would mean a fortune, and a fine laboratory too. Marie made no attempt to argue: she guessed he had raised the patent only out of scruple. Then, Ève writes, "in the silence Pierre repeated, like an echo," her phrase. A quarter of an hour later they were cycling towards the woods.
A fortune was given away in fifteen minutes and almost without words. This is the bright side of The Hermit at the entry: trust, agreements, an understanding that needs no argument.

The same entry has a reverse side. When fame came to the Curies, Pierre wrote to a friend: "We have never been less tranquil than at this moment. There are days when we scarcely have time to breathe. And to think that we dreamed of living in the wild, quite removed from human beings!" The dream a couple enters the task with becomes the yardstick by which every guest is an intrusion.

In a couple today this looks ordinary. At the start there is a sweet agreement: holidays for two, no noisy crowds, "we don't need anyone." Years later the same agreement turns a friend's invitation into a small betrayal and a partner's new interest into an escape from the shared home. The wish for quiet that brought the couple together starts to resist everything that does not fit into that quiet.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: the shed where things glowed
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya the middle of the task (N) has no meaning of its own; it is an addition to the main task. We read it as the path from the wish at the entry to the task: what the couple does and what it goes through. With The Hermit in the middle, the path runs through a long shared work in which each has a place, and closeness is expressed in deeds.

For the Curies that work was a shed in the courtyard of the School of Physics and Chemistry on the rue Lhomond in Paris, once a dissecting room. The glass roof leaked, in summer it was as stifling as a hothouse, and in winter only an iron stove gave any warmth. For four years Marie processed tons of uranium ore residues, spending whole days stirring a boiling mass with "a heavy iron rod nearly as large as myself", while Pierre studied the properties of the new radiation. "Yet it was in this miserable old shed that we passed the best and happiest years of our life," she would write. And one more line that answers the letter of 1894: "We lived in a preoccupation as complete as that of a dream." The wish to "pass through life side by side, hypnotized by our dreams" came true literally, in a shed with a leaking roof.

One evening in 1902, once radium had at last been obtained, Marie put their daughter to bed, sat down to hem the child's apron and could not settle: "Suppose we go down there for a moment?" Pierre wanted the same. They went on foot, arm in arm, exchanging few words. In the dark shed Marie said: "Don't light the lamps!" — and added with a little laugh: "Do you remember the day when you said to me: 'I should like radium to have a beautiful colour'?" Radium turned out to have no beautiful colour. It had something better: it glowed by itself. On the tables and shelves the tubes and dishes shimmered, "gleamings, which seemed suspended in the darkness", as Marie remembered. She found a straw-bottomed chair and sat down, leaning forward, just as she had sat an hour earlier by the bed of her sleeping child. Pierre's hand lightly touched her hair.

The whole middle of the tail is in this scene. The wish the couple started with comes true, but not as planned: not as a beautiful colour in daylight, but as a faint glow you can see only when the lamps are out. What the couple makes together goes unnoticed from outside — by guests, by family, even by the couple itself in the bustle of the day. It shows in the evening, when it is dark outside and words are not needed.

Today it might be a house that two people spend years renovating with their own hands, or two books written at neighbouring desks, or a garden, or a shared project that friends hear about only once it is finished. Love here speaks the language of deeds: tea brought in without a word, a shelf fixed, a draft read to the last page.

The downside of the middle is that the work becomes the only form of closeness. Even on cycling trips through the Cévennes and the Auvergne, after a few days Pierre would start to say: "It seems to me a very long time since we have accomplished anything." If the shared shed is the only place where a couple is truly together, then a holiday, a day off and any pause in the work feel like separation.

sections.h2: The Moon in the centre: a secret known to two
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the shared atmosphere, what is inside the couple and not on show. In 92.3% of couples with the 9-9-9 tail, The Moon is there.

Wen draws a distinction that fits here perfectly. The High Priestess, she writes, is personal mystery: "secrets that a person is withholding". The Moon is the mystery of nature: "secrets of the natural world, the hidden condition of the Seeker's situation that will reveal itself in time". For the Curies this was literal: their work began with invisible rays that Henri Becquerel found in a dark desk drawer in 1896. It was a cloudy February, he thought the experiment would not work without sunlight and put his photographic plates and uranium salt away to wait for clear weather — and when he developed them, he found a sharp image.

The atmosphere between the Curies was lunar too. Ève writes that Marie could talk about her work with only one person: "To him alone could she confide rare thoughts and dreams." To everyone else, even those dearest to her, she presented "an almost commonplace picture of herself", wrote about her work in "news in three lines", "concealed herself, dug herself in" — "she offered only one of her profiles". A world known to two, and a calm mask for everyone else.

On the bright side, The Moon in the centre is intuition. The partner is a friend first of all; they understand each other without explanations, respect each other's space and every year discover something new in the other. In Pierre's letter, the first promise was precisely friendship: "at least a great friendship."

On the dark side, The Moon does with the silence of three Hermits what it does best: it fills it with imagination. One partner is silent because they are thinking about work. In the meantime the other manages to invent what the silence is about, take offence at the imagined answer and fall silent too. Both are sure they have understood each other without words. Neither has checked.

For this atmosphere Lisovskaya gives a piece of advice that a 9-9-9 couple could not find more precise: accept that the partner sometimes needs to withdraw into themselves — it is their way of recovering, not a lack of love. And one more: do not think for the other person.

If the centre is not The Moon but The Hermit (7.7% of couples), imagination is quieter, but another risk is stronger: each has their own corner, the corners slowly drift apart, and one day each finds themselves on their own.

sections.h2: Main task: noticing the one beside you
paragraphs: The main task (D) is the couple's chief trial, and it is read mostly through its shadow side: what the couple does not manage and what it has to learn. The Hermit here is not the quiet itself but what gets lost in it.

Before the wedding Marie secretly took cookery lessons from her sister and her sister's mother-in-law, and later filled the margins of her cookbook with notes "of scientific accuracy" on her trials, failures and successes. Pierre, Ève writes, was "so absent-minded that he never even noticed the great effort she made". She did not say. He did not see. There is no culprit in this scene: there is a silence in which one person's effort is invisible to the other. With The Hermit in the main task, grievances and problems pile up exactly like this — silently, until they grow too big simply to be mentioned.

The second scene is the reverse. Pierre, in his daughter's words, was "the most possessive and jealous of husbands": he was so used to his wife's constant presence that "her least eclipse kept him from thinking freely". When Marie lingered upstairs with four-year-old Irène, he met her with a reproach "so unjust as to be comic": "You never think of anything but that child!" A solitude for two is built for exactly two. A third — a child, a friend, a project of one's own, a trip to see parents — feels like an eclipse.

The third scene is the main one. In 1903 the French Academy of Sciences nominated Henri Becquerel and Pierre Curie for the Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was not named. The Swedish mathematician Gösta Mittag-Leffler warned Pierre, and he replied: "If it is true that one is seriously thinking about me, I very much wish to be considered together with Madame Curie with respect to our research on radioactive bodies." The prize was shared: half went to Becquerel, half to Monsieur and Madame Curie.

This letter holds what the main task of 9-9-9 teaches. Inside a quiet couple it goes without saying that the work is shared. From outside this cannot be seen, and the world readily sees one lamp instead of two. Lisovskaya writes that in a Hermit couple one partner may become well known and the other turn into their shadow, and the first of The Hermit's tasks on her list is not to dampen a partner's interest in their own pursuits. Pierre had to say out loud what had never been said in their shed: "together". Even here his wife is "Madame Curie": The Hermit says "together" without a single word to spare.

Fame brought the next trial. The day after the ceremony they did not attend, Marie wrote to her brother: "We are inundated with letters and with visits from photographers and journalists. One would like to dig into the ground somewhere to find a little peace." The papers reported their daughter's conversation with her nurse and described the black-and-white cat. Later Marie would call it the overturn of their "voluntary isolation", which "had all the effect of disaster". Hiding from the world together is easy, and that is not the task of the tail. The task is not to hide from each other: in hard times not to retreat each into themselves but to help, to share and to listen, to sense when to support the partner and when to leave them in peace.

This task has a quiet answer too. When the Curies found their first new element in 1898, Pierre said to his wife: "You will have to name it." Marie called it polonium, and the paper for the Academy reads: "from the name of the original country of one of us." Even in that summer letter of 1894 Pierre had not made her dream a shared one: "your dream for your country, our dream for humanity, our dream for science." Inside the "we" there was room left for "one of us". The main task of 9-9-9 is to keep that room: each with a work, a country, a friend of their own — and none of it a betrayal of the shared solitude.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: words that came true
paragraphs: In Waite's divinatory list The Hermit reads: "Prudence, circumspection; also and especially treason, dissimulation, roguery, corruption." Reversed: "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution."

The Curies' story echoes this list twice. Where Ève describes how her mother hid her work from everyone but her husband, the English edition of the book says that Marie "concealed herself" and "dissimulated herself" behind "a woman like all others". This is not deceit but modesty and, in her daughter's words, a "horror of vain talk". Yet the words are the same as in Waite's list: in The Hermit, concealment is the other face of prudence.

The second word is "corruption". In the preface to the same book Ève quotes Einstein: "Marie Curie is, of all celebrated beings, the only one whom fame has not corrupted." The English text uses the very word that stands in The Hermit's list: corrupted. Solitude protected her from what Waite calls corruption — and charged its price in concealment.

Waite himself saw The Hermit as a card of attainment: a figure on a height holds up a lantern in which a star shines, and, unlike in older decks, the lamp is not wrapped in the mantle. For a couple this is the difference between a door and a lamp. The Curies' house on the boulevard Kellermann was closed: from the street there was only a blank wall and a tiny door, with the garden hidden behind the house. But they did not hide their light. "No detail was kept secret," Marie wrote about the process for preparing radium, and she told an American journalist: "Radium is an element. It belongs to all people." A closed door and an open lamp — the strongest version of three Hermits.

Wen adds one more trait to the portrait: The Hermit "walks in the direction of his own thoughts only; he is not a traditionalist". A wedding without a ring, a honeymoon on bicycles, a husband who asks for his wife to share the prize — a couple of Hermits rarely lives "the proper way". It does not need to become like everyone else. It needs not to become impenetrable to each other.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the work or the dream
paragraphs: In these couples the couple's values are either The Hermit again (59.3%) or The Moon (40.7%). There is no third option: what this union exists for is decided by the same two cards that already stand in the tail and in the centre.

Our reading: The Hermit in the values is a union for the sake of depth itself — for knowledge, mastery, a shared work bigger than both. The Moon in the values is a union for the sake of a shared inner world: a dream, imagination, what two people see alike when they close their eyes. Pierre's letter holds both. He lists three dreams and at once picks one: "Of all these dreams, I believe the last, alone, is legitimate" — the dream of science, where "however small it is, it is truly in our possession." The work. Polonium shows that the dream did not go anywhere either. It helps a couple to know which of the two cards stands in its values: whether it is together for the work or for the dream. That decides what it would be more afraid to lose.

sections.h2: How to step out of the 9-9-9 tail: a third chair at the table
paragraphs: Stepping out of the tail does not mean falling out of love with quiet. Quiet is this couple's strength. Stepping out means no longer hiding from each other inside it. Here are habits that change the script:

ul: **Say out loud what is visible without words.** "I can see how much went into this" weighs more than one more silent cup of tea. In this couple, what is not said does not exist for the other person.
**Give notice when withdrawing.** "I need to think; I'm not walking away from you" — one sentence is enough to leave The Moon in the centre nothing to make up.
**Ask instead of guessing.** If the partner seems hurt, ask. A guessed answer is almost always darker than the real one.
**Talk about difficulties before they are solved.** "It's all sorted already" sounds like "we managed without you."
**Leave room for "one of us".** A work of one's own, a friend of one's own, a trip to see one's parents take nothing away from the shared solitude.
**Put a third chair at the table.** Let people into the house now and then — guests, friends, students. To two Hermits this feels like a sacrifice, but otherwise there is no one to see their light.
**Rest without a report on what got done.** A day when the two of them "accomplished nothing" is still a day together.

paragraphs: The strong version of the 9-9-9 tail is a couple whose quiet produces light, not walls. Two people at one table, each at their own end, and one lamp in the middle that lights both pages at once. The world may make out only one of them. The couple's task is for each to see both.

The person born on 17.01.1976 has the personal tail 15-20-5; the person born on 14.04.1975 has 12-16-4. This is the most common combination that adds up to 9-9-9, and neither personal tail contains a nine or an eighteen.

The couple's centre is The Moon: one partner's Wheel of Fortune and the other's Justice, 10 + 8 = 18. This is also the most common case: in 58% of couples with the 9-9-9 tail the partners' personal centres are 8 and 10. The couple's values are The Hermit, 9.

In this example The Hermit occupies eight of the sixteen points of the reading. Besides the three points of the tail and the values, these are "What fills" (18 + 18 = 36 → 9), "Home and things" (5 + 22 = 27 → 9), "Path to prosperity" (18 + 18 = 36 → 9) and "What connects" (18 + 9 = 27 → 9). The Moon stands in two more places: "Way into money" (15 + 3 = 18) and "Success and the union" (3 + 15 = 18). Usually there are fewer such points: in 70% of couples with this tail, 9 and 18 stand on exactly five points — in the tail, the centre and the values.

What shows on the outside is curious. Here "Image of the couple" is The Emperor (17 + 14 = 31 → 4) and "What to create together" is The Hierophant (1 + 4 = 5): the same two cards of order that stand in the partners' personal main tasks. Outside, rules and structure; inside, three Hermits. And even these two cards add up to 4 + 5 = 9.

intro: The three Hermits stand in three different places, and each has its own role:

ul: **M · Entry to the task — The Hermit.** The couple is drawn together by a wish for quiet and depth. Their common language is understanding without unnecessary words and an unspoken agreement: "the two of us are enough."
**N · Middle of the task — The Hermit.** The path runs through a long shared work. Each has a place and a time of their own, and love shows in deeds rather than declarations.
**D · Main task — The Hermit.** Learning to speak inside the shared quiet: noticing each other's effort, not letting one light block out the other, and not turning solitude into a fortress.

intro: What this looks like in real life is best seen in one famous couple. Marie Curie called the life she shared with Pierre a "voluntary isolation", and both described it in such detail that the three nines can be read in their letters one after another. But first, a clue in the numbers themselves: a Moon that has gone missing from the middle of the tail.

faq.q: What does the 9-9-9 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail in which all three points — the entry to the task, the middle and the main task — are held by The Hermit. The couple comes together over a wish for quiet and depth, lives it out through a long shared work, and its main task is not to hide from each other inside the shared solitude: to speak, to share and not to block each other out.

faq.q: Why does the 9-9-9 tail never appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is calculated from its ends: the entry plus the main task. With nines at both ends the middle is always 9 + 9 = 18, so a single person gets 9-18-9. In a couple the middle is the sum of the two partners' middles, and it can stay a nine.

faq.q: Is a couple with the 9-9-9 tail doomed to loneliness?
faq.a: No. The tail predicts nothing and passes no verdicts. It describes a task: the couple knows how to create a shared quiet, and its trial is for each partner to stay visible to the other inside that quiet. Solitude for two and loneliness for two are separated by the words that get said out loud.

faq.q: Neither of our personal tails has a nine — is that a mistake?
faq.a: No, that is how it is for most: in 79% of couples with the 9-9-9 tail, neither partner has a 9 or an 18 in their personal tail. The Hermit forms from numbers that complete each other to a nine, such as 12 + 15, 16 + 20 and 4 + 5. It appears only in the couple.

faq.q: How can you calculate a couple's tail yourself?
faq.a: Take the three points of each partner's personal tail — the entry, the middle and the karmic task — and add the matching ones: entry to entry, middle to middle, task to task. A sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits: 27 → 9, 36 → 9. The couple's middle is not recalculated from its ends.

report: No single person can have three Hermits in a row: in a personal matrix The Moon always stands between two nines. The 9-9-9 tail occurs only in a couple — and most often in two people whose personal tails hold neither The Hermit nor The Moon. Each number of one partner completes the other's number to a nine, and two tails full of drama and rules add up to quiet. **Neither of the two brings this quiet along: it appears only when they are together.** Hence the couple's main task — not to hide from each other inside it.

The Moon does not vanish, though. There was no room for it in the middle of the tail, so in these couples it almost always moves to the centre — into the atmosphere, into what happens between the partners when nobody is watching.

report.h3: Two chairs and none for a guest

report: This tail is best explained by the story of a couple whose shared life Marie Curie called a "voluntary isolation". A solitude for two is built for exactly two.

In 1903 Pierre was nominated for the Nobel Prize and Marie was not named. He replied that he "very much wished to be considered together with Madame Curie". **Inside a quiet couple it goes without saying that the work is shared; from outside, the world readily sees one lamp instead of two.** The task of 9-9-9 is to say out loud what was never said in the shared shed: "together". And to leave room inside the "we" for each: Marie named her first new element polonium, "from the name of the original country of one of us."

report.h3: A closed door and an open lamp

report: Einstein said: "Marie Curie is, of all celebrated beings, the only one whom fame has not corrupted." In Waite, "corruption" stands in The Hermit's list — next to "concealment" and "dissimulation", the very words her daughter used for how Marie hid her work from everyone but her husband. Solitude protects, and charges a price for it. From the street the Curies' house was shut off by a blank wall, yet they did not keep a single detail of the radium process secret. **A closed door and an open lamp — the strongest version of three Hermits.**

Stepping out of the tail does not mean falling out of love with quiet: quiet is this couple's strength. Stepping out means no longer hiding from each other inside it. Saying out loud what is visible without words. Giving notice when withdrawing to think, rather than walking away from the partner. Asking instead of guessing. Talking about difficulties before they are solved. Now and then, putting a third chair at the table.
Two people at one table, each at their own end, and one lamp in the middle lights both pages at once. The world may make out only one of them. The couple's task is for each to see both.
